name: Articos MCP
tagline: See how simulated buyers react, right in your agent
description: Most teams ship, then hope it lands. Articos MCP lets you check first. Right inside Claude or ChatGPT, run your headlines, positioning, or pages past simulated buyers based on your actual customers, and see how they respond before it goes out. Validated against human research from Baymard and Nielsen Norman, it agrees 86% of the time.

nodes.body: This sounds great. But like a lot of folks are asking, across different personas, can you still validate against actual human taste?
testing ideas on simulated buyers inside the agent is a usefull idea 🙌 how close do they match real customers?

Coming from ad ops, the gap I see most is between copy that tests well and what the ad platform’s delivery actually rewards. Do you let users feed real campaign results back in, like CTR or CVR by headline, so the simulated buyers get calibrated to their own account over time?

So I actually use this to settle arguments with my cofounder about button colors and other things. It is of annoying because sometimes the bot persona gets fixated on random words in our drafts and just ignores the main layout. We end up spending twenty minutes arguing with a buyer, about font sizes.

This whole simulated buyer concept feels like an echo chamber that simply repeats your own marketing ideas. You upload customer data and the LLM suddenly says your new landing page is a winner.. What exactly happens to the proprietary persona data that we send to their servers? What does the LLM do with that persona data once it lands on their servers?
do you plan to validate the product's predictions against the live A/B tests? for example, by running the same messaging tests with simulated audiences and real users.

Testing messaging is one of those things every team agrees they should do, but just doesn't happen right up until a launch deadline 😅

Making it possible to pressure-test a positioning change in the middle of the workflow is a very very interesting use of MCP.
@chrismessina Can't wait to try it, we are constantly testing our LP's for the right kind of audience. Will share my review here.
It saves you so much time and guessing when you test your messaging before spending money on launching it.

I believe that verifying the messaging or presentation of something before bringing it to market is a truly effective idea. Even a slight change in how a product is portrayed can lead to a significant difference in peoples perception of it. Moreover, integrating this process into the relevant team's existing workflow makes the concept even more appealing.

The concept of simulated customer feedback seems quite intriguing. I am interested to know how Articos handles products with multiple customer segments especially when a single message might appeal to one group while having no impact on another. Can users compare these reactions side by side?

Congrats Shaheer and Owais on the MCP launch. The pitch that you can stay inside Claude, draft a headline, and get ICP-matched pushback before shipping is clear. One edge I keep hitting in practice: after two or three rewrite rounds in the same chat, do the personas stay frozen, or can a later prompt quietly drift the ICP so the third test is no longer comparable to the first?

This is the kind of MCP that doubles or triples the value and convenience of a product like this. 

By being able to pull in your Articos synthetic audiences into your chat agent, you can connect to the data, marketing materials, and related content right from the conversations you already have going on. 

Brilliant!
ICP is where I would use this tbh. we always think we know our buyers and then the data says otherwise. Can you pressure test that too, or is it more for messaging?
i am really into claude all day and bringing my buyers into my agent is just amazing but i wonder what would be the the quality and how close they are ?
Pre-launch page copy is where I stall — MCP-in-chat for a quick headline gut-check sounds useful. Congrats on the launch.

I'm tightening a pre-launch page and keep second-guessing headline vs sub — the MCP-in-chat angle sounds useful so I'm not jumping out of Claude to sanity-check copy. Have you tried it on a "who is this for" line before the main CTA?
Interesting product, I will be using this test it for my launches.

Love the idea behind Articos , Being able to validate messaging and positioning with simulated buyers directly inside Claude or ChatGPT before launching could save teams a lot of guesswork. The 86% human accuracy claim is especially interesting. Congrats on the launch, and wishing the team great success!

name: Muse Wonder
tagline: Meta’s most capable models for personal agents
description: Muse Wonder is Meta’s new model series for personal and professional agents, with two models: Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full. Active Memory carries your context across conversations, Active Focus keeps working through blockers on hard goals, and it adds domain expertise in law, finance, and health plus stronger coding. Muse Wonder is live on the Meta Model API and Muse Code. Muse Wonder Full is for Muse Code subscribers.

nodes.body:
Muse Wonder is Meta’s new model series for personal and professional agents, from Meta AI Research. It has two models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full. Meta calls them its most capable models, and the post says they were trained at its Prometheus data center.

Problem: Most AI assistants forget you between chats and give up or drift on long, hard tasks. The post frames personal agents as needing to remember context, stay on a goal and handle private information carefully.

Solution: Meta built the series around four things:

  • Active Memory: carries important context about you across conversations and pulls up the relevant details for the current task

  • Active Focus: keeps working toward a hard goal by trying other approaches and working through blockers, and asks for clarification or checks in before important actions

  • Domain expertise: specialized knowledge in law, finance and health, such as understanding a lease

  • Frontier coding: tracks requirements, edits codebases and iterates through testing cycles, trained on long-running tasks

What makes it different: the focus on long-running, personal work. Meta shows demos like a Saturday run plan built across a browser and other apps, custom swag ordered from Instagram photos, and a playable 3D kitchen game built from image inputs. You can try the Kitchen Game demo and the step-and-repeat demo.

How it performs: Meta says it reaches state-of-the-art results on benchmarks for personal and professional agents, memory and coding. The named evaluations are Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark, FocusBench and SWE-Marathon. These are Meta’s own claims, and the post’s text gives no scores, since the comparisons are in charts. The model report has the full evaluation details.

Availability:

  • Muse Wonder is available now through the Meta Model API and Muse Code

  • Muse Wonder Full is available now for Muse Code subscribers

  • The Muse app will soon be powered by Muse Wonder, rolling out first to subscribers

Safety: Meta says it has its strongest safeguards to date against chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear and cyber misuse, under its Superintelligence Scaling Framework.

Who it’s for: developers building agents through the API or Muse Code, and people who want a personal assistant that keeps context over time.

Read the full announcement.

name: Kai
tagline: Autonomous assistant designed to handle meetings and email
description: Kai is an AI executive assistant for solopreneurs, freelancers and startup founders. It works across your email, calendar and tasks: it triages your inbox and drafts replies, schedules around your availability, records and transcribes your meetings, then turns them into summaries and action items. Workflows run in the background, and Kai hands tasks to Claude or ChatGPT with the context of the meeting or email they came from. Web, desktop and mobile. Product Hunt sign-ups get 2x trial credits.

nodes.body:
Hey Product Hunt 👋

Today we’re launching Kai, and I want to share a bit about why we built it.

Every founder and team lead has two jobs!

We’ve spent more than five years in productivity building Morgen, and we kept hearing the same thing from founders and team leads. They all juggle two jobs:

  1. The job they were hired to do

  2. Everything around it: managing coordination across people, the back-and-forth, jumping between calls, scheduling meetings, answering emails, chasing people

The second job quietly eats the first one. We built Kai for the second job.

Why now

AI tools like Claude and ChatGPT get more capable every month. But they still wait for you to ask, and they don’t really know you. They don’t see the promise you made on Tuesday’s call, the reply you’re still waiting on, or the clash hiding in next week’s calendar. That context lives in your meetings, your email and your calendar, and that’s exactly where Kai works.

Honestly, I’m sick of hearing about CLIs, MCPs and connected workflows. I just wanted to build an extremely simple, delightful personal assistant that gives people back hours every day, without asking them to become prompt engineers.

AI deserves a real interface

I’m a big UI and UX nerd. Every AI product I’ve tried was either a chat bar stuck onto an existing app, or a plain chat with almost no interface. We set out to make Kai the first AI that gets both right: an agent you can talk to, and a UI that’s a joy to use.

So Kai doesn’t wait to be asked. It shows up with a question and a fix ready:

📩 “Jim wants to push the 2:00 investor call by 30 minutes. You’re free at 2:30. Should I move it and draft a reply?” One tap, and you press Send.

🎙️ You say “I’ll build the Q3 deck tonight” on a call, and it’s on your task list before you hang up, ready to hand to Claude with the meeting context attached.

☀️ You ask the same question every morning, and Kai offers to just brief you at 8 am instead.

Nothing goes out without you. Kai drafts; you press Send.

Where we’re going

This is day one. Over the next 12 months we’re doubling down on three things: making Kai more proactive, making the experience even more delightful, and expanding what it can take off your plate.

Try it today 🎁

Kai is free to start on Web, Mac, iPhone, and Android at hirekai.ai (every Product Hunter who signs up today gets 2x the trial credits!).

I’ll be here all day reading every comment, and I’d love to know: what’s the part of your “second job” you’d hand to Kai first? 👇

David

PS: A huge shoutout to our hundreds of beta users who've showered us with love and feedback over the last few months. We wouldn’t be here without you!

Kai has been really great for me. I have ADHD and it has really handled a lot of my executive function challenges. As an early tester, I have seen Kai develop and refine and features continue to be added to improve functionality and flexibility. The iPhone app is superb (still in beta).

This is an app that is not just for entrepreneurs - its for all kinds of busy professionals. I'm a health, safety and wellbeing consultant, and it helps me keep on top of things and juggle.

Congratulations! Can’t wait to try KAI out in my law practice.

Super happy and proud of the journey we've had the past 8 months to give birth to Kai. This will only be the start of Kai's takeover >:)

Hope everyone has a good time with Kai!

The example where Kai sees that Jim wants to push the investor call and already has the new time and a draft reply ready is the part that sold me. That is the difference between an assistant that waits for a prompt and one that actually watches your calendar and inbox. I have lost real hours to exactly that kind of back and forth over email! That context is usually where my own replies go wrong.

I've always loved what the Kai team built with Morgen, and although i've got the technical know-how to connect up all my tools, when @dannyhatcher introduced me to what the team were making I was like... oh I can just do the things.

Now I use Kai for a variety of things, Inbox Management, Food Prep, Study Sessions... Medicine Reminders for all the things you know you've gotta do... but always end up being a little bit slippy.

It's just nice to have a single place to go to be able to check my calendar, emails and tasks without having to think about the connective tissue behind it.

That plus the fact there's an MCP so I can connect with my local agents, means that there's an easy customisable pipeline for me to do the work i gotta do, whilst also juggling life admin, looking after two children, and running a business with multiple moving parts at the same time.

The clean interface that just works means I don't have to think about how to make it work... it learns what I do, and makes it possible without having to futz around with connectors or... anything else technical... if you don't wanna.

Sure productivity is great and all... but frankly just being able to send a quick message to remember something whilst cooking food and my children ask me for something... and it just appears scheduled in my calendar makes things far faaar easier than it ever used to be....

And unlike other tools that say they do the same things as Kai... They are just missing the features or the UI that makes sense for how I work.

Hi everyone,

I’m Marco, CTO at Kai. First, a big thank you to our entire team. I’m proud of what we’ve achieved together.

Kai could build on the battle-tested infrastructure of Morgen, our daily planner used by thousands of people every day. Even so, building Kai brought its own set of challenges:

  • Balancing text and visual interfaces. Text is common and expressive, but often hard to digest. Sometimes pressing a button is faster than chatting, so we wanted Kai to offer whichever UX fits each use case best. With Kai, we wanted to reduce the number of tools you need to look at, not add one more. In fact, I think you won't need to look at your Gmail or Outlook anymore.

  • Answering with depth, breadth, and speed. An agent building a product can happily work in the background for half an hour. We wanted Kai to be snappy, like a real assistant. More easily said than done, given the current state of the technology, yet I think we achieved our goal here.

  • Aggregating information efficiently, securely, and effectively. Kai connects the dots between what was said in a meeting and the emails that follow on the same topic weeks later. It also keeps track of your preferences and adapts to your preferred workflows.

We’re just getting started and I hope you like what we are building. Give it a try and let us know what you think!

name: MentionBird
tagline: Ahrefs for AI Search
description: We took the top 3 Product Hunt launches and asked ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude the exact questions their buyers ask: “Best browser for Claude Code?” “How do I track agent run costs?” “Best open-source Grok alternative?” Nine answers. Zero mentions. AI sent their buyers elsewhere. That’s how AI search works. It pulls from pages it trusts—listicles, Reddit, comparisons, YouTube. If you’re not there, you’re not in the answer. MentionBird helps you fix that.

nodes.body:
Hey Product Hunt, I'm Salil, maker of MentionBird.

I spent a decade helping brands get found on Google. Then buyers started asking ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity "what's the best X for Y" instead, and most brands had no idea what AI was saying about them. When they checked, the answer usually stung: years of Google rankings, and still not named.

AI answers aren't built from your rankings. They're built from the sources AI trusts: review sites, listicles, forums, publications. If you're not in those, you're not in the answer.

MentionBird makes that visible and fixable:
- Enter your company and URL, and it finds the buying questions that matter in your category
- It tracks daily which brands ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Claude name in their answers, and which sources those answers are built on
- The Answer Agent turns that into a ranked action plan: which sources to get into, what to publish or fix, ordered by impact and effort

Recently shipped: a rebuilt Answer Agent and a new YouTube Answer Agent.

For the Product Hunt community: your first 3 months of Starter is $19 with code PH19.

I'd love to hear from you: which AI answer in your category would you most want to win?

How do you handle prompt wording? The same buyer question phrased two ways can name completely different brands, so I'm curious how many variants you track per question before calling something a trend

Congrats on the launch — the "Ahrefs for AI Search" framing clicked instantly.

We checked our own AI referrals recently, and the honest numbers are humbling: single-digit sessions a week. Easy to dismiss at that size, but worth tracking anyway.

One GA4 gotcha we hit that others here might too: the "AI Assistant" channel group only catches part of the picture — our chatgpt.com sessions show up there, but Perplexity and Copilot land in plain "Referral", so channel-level views undercount AI traffic. Reading session source/medium directly is what surfaced ours. If you surface source-level splits, that distinction will save people real confusion.

Or must you add competitors yourself in order to track them? I'm thinking of local service businesses, like a plumber for example. They might not know who to compare themselves to, or they might input competitors who aren't ranking either, so their own picks wouldn't help as much as if MentionBird suggested some. Congrats on a great tool at a great time!

name: MausBot
tagline: Open source Grok Bot: Free, Local
description: Give each bot a job and work with it in a familiar chat interface. MausBot brings your supported AI agents together on your computer, with tools and routines for getting work done. Free and open source under Apache 2.0. Bring your own provider account or API key; provider fees and limits apply.

nodes.body:
Hey Product Hunt! 👋 I’m Omkar, building MausBot with Milind and our open-source contributors.

MausBot is a free, open-source Grokbot alternative: your own team of AI bots, in a chat app.

We open-sourced MausBot about two hours after Grokbot officially launched. We were already building something similar, and seeing the launch gave us the push to share our work, make it open source, and keep building with the community.

The idea behind MausBot is simple: your own team of AI bots, in a chat app. Give each bot a job, choose its model, and keep its conversations and work together.

With MausBot, you can:

- Run bots in parallel for research, writing, and coding.
- Use Claude, Codex, and other supported engines in one app.
- Connect tools like GitHub, Gmail, and Slack.
- Let bots work on your Mac or a connected cloud desktop, with permissions and approval settings you control.

For example, ask one bot to turn customer feedback into a prioritized engineering brief, then ask another to investigate a reported bug in your repository. Review their work and decide what happens next.

We’re continuing to build toward that experience, with the code open for anyone to inspect, modify, and contribute to.

The app is free and open source under Apache 2.0. Bring a supported AI account or API key; provider fees and limits apply. Paid cloud hosting is optional.

Try it: https://mausbot.com
Source: https://github.com/milind-soni/O...

Hi, I'm Rowland, Genchi's founder.

Genchi shows engineering leaders a prediction of which projects are heading for a missed deadline and which aren't, from the people doing the work. Giving every engineer a way to be heard, this prediction comes from their anonymous, one-click confidence vote in response to a regular, automated Slack prompt. Why another tool?

Standups (and standup tools) are intra-team focused. They tell a team how the team is doing, and often perform a "status thumb check," but that view rarely travels beyond the team.

Developer Productivity Insight Platforms are analytical. They forecast from work already completed, so they can't see what hasn't reached the tracker yet: the vague requirement, the shaky dependency, the worry nobody has raised.

Genchi makes it easy to capture the signal directly from the people doing the work. Think of a rolling SAFe confidence vote (fist of five), from 1 (Doubtful) to 5 (Certain), combined by project and visualized across the portfolio.

I first launched Genchi here in 2021, and it was stalled by COVID. This is a complete rebuild, with Jira and Asana integrations and an MCP App that shows your live portfolio inside Claude, ChatGPT and Grok.

name: Upsolve Row-Level Security
tagline: Data permissions your AI agent can't talk its way past
description: Row-level security enforced server side, before any query runs. Set rules from user and org properties, test them as any user, and deploy one agent to thousands of tenants. The agent never sees the rules, so it can't bypass them.

nodes.body:
Hey Product Hunt, Ka Ling from Upsolve AI.

The first question every security team asks about a data agent is: what stops it from showing one customer another customer's data? If your answer is "the prompt", you don't have an answer.

Upsolve Row-Level Security takes permissions out of the agent entirely. You register orgs and users with properties like country or tenant ID, then set global rules (column country = user.country) or write your own SQL rules per table. Every query, whether the agent or a person wrote it, gets pre-filtered on the server before it runs. The agent never even sees the rules.

You can test any rule as any user before you ship. In the demo, Grace sees four APAC countries and Carlos sees only Brazil, from the same agent.
This is what lets you put one agent in front of thousands of tenants. How are you handling permissions for AI features today?

Hi ! sharing live numbers with customers always gave me a small knot in my stomach, that worry someone catches a figure meant for another account. This is the kind of thing that'd let me relax about it.

Ka Ling, testing a rule as a particular user before shipping it stood out to me. Much easier to check what a customer will actually see when the permissions are enforced before the query runs. Congrats on the launch!

We run AI agents for many stores, and keeping one store's customers away from another store's agent is the one thing I would never leave to the model. One question: the rules are on tables and columns. What happens when the agent calls a tool or an API instead of writing SQL, say fetching an order from Shopify? Is that outside what this covers?

"If your answer is the prompt, you don't have an answer" is spot on. Same thing goes for quality: you enforce it in infrastructure, you don't ask for it in a CLAUDE.md. Do you log denied queries back to the agent so it learns the boundary, or does it stay invisible to it?

nodes.body:
Hi everyone, I'm Varun. OpenFlowKit was here about 8 months ago as v1. Version 2 is a rebuild from scratch:

- One canvas, five ways in: draw it, write it as code, ask any AI model (or a local one), hand it to your coding agent, or pull it from a GitHub repo
- Your coding agent edits the canvas you have open, live, over MCP (npx -y openflowkit mcp). Every change is one undo step
- Text and canvas are the same diagram: write it as code, or paste Mermaid, D2 or Structurizr
- The repo map cites the file and line behind every arrow, so you can check it instead of trusting it

Why I built it: every team I've worked on had an architecture diagram that was right once. The code kept moving, the diagram didn't, and new people learned the system from a picture nobody trusted. So everything here is built to keep the diagram current: you, your AI and your agent all edit the same one.

Try it with no account: app.openflowkit.com

Honest limits: the map reads code statically (imports and config files, not running traffic), reads public GitHub repos in the browser (run the CLI on a checkout for private ones), and is weaker on .NET and Elixir projects without containers. There's no real-time collaboration yet.

It's free and MIT licensed, and I built it on my own.

A real question: what's the diagram you keep redrawing? Try it there and tell me what got in the way.

The one I keep redrawing is which service is allowed to touch which table, and static imports is exactly where that one falls over. An import graph tells you what can call what, not what does, so the edges I care about are the ones that only exist at runtime, a queue, a webhook, a cron job hitting an endpoint nobody imports. Drift check will happily tell me the diagram is current while the edge that would actually hurt me was never on it. Worth saying you listed that limit yourself, most launches bury it.
